paragraphs: After parting from Alyosha, Ivan went home to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. But strangely, he was overcome by an unbearable depression, which grew worse with every step he took toward the house. There was nothing strange in his being depressed. What was strange was that Ivan could not say what caused it. He had often been depressed before, and it was no surprise that he felt so now, when he had broken with everything that had brought him here and was getting ready to make a new start that very day and step into a new, unknown future. He would be as solitary as ever. He had great hopes, and great—too great—expectations of life, yet he could not have given any clear account of his hopes, his expectations, or even his desires.

Still, though he certainly felt some dread of the new and unknown, what was worrying him at that moment was something quite different. “Is it loathing for my father’s house?” he wondered. “Quite likely. I am so sick of it, and though this is the last time I will cross its hateful threshold, I still loathe it.... No, it’s not that either. Is it the parting with Alyosha, and the conversation I had with him? For so many years I’ve kept silent with the whole world and not bothered to speak, and all of a sudden I reel off a rigmarole like that.” It might well have been the youthful vexation of youthful inexperience and vanity—vexation at having failed to express himself, especially to someone like Alyosha, on whom his heart had certainly been counting. No doubt that played a part, that vexation, it must have done; and yet that was not it, that was not it either. “I feel sick with depression and yet I can’t tell what I want. Better not to think, perhaps.”

Ivan tried “not to think,” but that was no use either. What made his depression so annoying and irritating was that it seemed to come from outside, by chance—he could feel that. Some person or thing seemed to be standing out there somewhere. It was like something that sometimes forces itself on the eye. One may be so busy with work or conversation that for a long time one does not notice it, yet it irritates and almost torments one, until at last one realizes what it is and removes the offending object, often something quite trifling and ridiculous—some article left in the wrong place, a handkerchief on the floor, a book not put back on the shelf, and so on.
At last, feeling very cross and in a foul mood, Ivan arrived home. About fifteen paces from the garden gate, he suddenly guessed what was fretting and worrying him.

On a bench in the gateway sat the valet Smerdyakov, enjoying the cool of the evening. At the first glance at him, Ivan knew that the valet Smerdyakov was what weighed on his mind, and that it was this man his soul loathed. It all dawned on him suddenly and became clear. Just before, when Alyosha had been telling him about his meeting with Smerdyakov, Ivan had felt a sudden twinge of gloom and loathing, which had immediately stirred an answering anger in his heart. Afterwards, as they talked, Smerdyakov had been forgotten for a time. But he had still been in Ivan’s mind, and as soon as Ivan parted from Alyosha and was walking home, the forgotten feeling began to push itself forward again. “Can it be that a miserable, contemptible creature like that worries me so much?” he wondered, in unbearable irritation.

It was true that Ivan had lately come to feel an intense dislike for the man, especially in the last few days. He had even begun to notice a growing feeling in himself that was almost hatred for the creature. Perhaps this hatred was sharpened by the fact that when Ivan first came to the neighborhood, he had felt quite differently. Then he had taken a marked interest in Smerdyakov, and had even thought him very original. He had encouraged him to talk, although he had always wondered at a certain incoherence, or rather restlessness, in his mind, and could not understand what it was that so constantly and insistently occupied the brain of “the contemplative.” They discussed philosophical questions, and even how there could have been light on the first day when the sun, moon, and stars were only created on the fourth day, and how that was to be understood. But Ivan soon saw that the sun, moon, and stars might be an interesting subject, yet were quite secondary to Smerdyakov, and that he was looking for something altogether different. One way and another, he began to show a boundless vanity, and a wounded vanity too, and Ivan disliked that. It was what first gave rise to his aversion. Later on there was trouble in the house. Grushenka appeared on the scene, and there were the scandals with his brother Dmitri—they discussed that too. But though Smerdyakov always talked of it with great excitement, it was impossible to discover what he wanted to come of it. There was, in fact, something surprising in the illogic and incoherence of some of his wishes, which he gave away by accident and always expressed vaguely. Smerdyakov was always inquiring, putting certain indirect but obviously planned questions, but he did not explain what he was after, and usually at the most important moment he would break off and fall silent or switch to another subject. But what finally irritated Ivan most and confirmed his dislike was the peculiar, revolting familiarity that Smerdyakov began to show more and more markedly. Not that he forgot himself and was rude. On the contrary, he always spoke very respectfully. Yet he had obviously begun to believe—goodness knows why!—that there was some sort of understanding between him and Ivan Fyodorovitch. He always spoke in a tone that suggested those two had some kind of compact, some secret between them, which had at some time been voiced on both sides, known only to them and beyond the comprehension of everyone around them. But for a long while Ivan did not recognize the real cause of his growing dislike, and only lately had he realized what lay at the root of it.

Feeling disgust and irritation, he tried to go in at the gate without speaking to Smerdyakov or looking at him. But Smerdyakov rose from the bench, and from that action alone Ivan knew at once that he particularly wanted to talk to him. Ivan looked at him and stopped. The fact that he did stop, instead of walking past as he had meant to a moment before, drove him to fury. With anger and repulsion he looked at Smerdyakov’s emasculate, sickly face, with the little curls combed forward on his forehead. His left eye winked and he grinned, as if to say, “Where are you going? You won’t pass by. You see that we two clever people have something to say to each other.”

Ivan shook. “Get away, you miserable idiot. What have I to do with you?” was on the tip of his tongue, but to his profound astonishment he heard himself say, “Is my father still asleep, or is he awake?”

He asked the question softly and meekly, to his own surprise, and at once, again to his own surprise, sat down on the bench. For an instant he felt almost frightened. He remembered it afterwards. Smerdyakov stood facing him, his hands behind his back, looking at him with assurance and almost severity.

“His honor is still asleep,” he said deliberately. (“You were the first to speak, not I,” he seemed to say.) “I am surprised at you, sir,” he added after a pause, dropping his eyes affectedly, setting his right foot forward, and playing with the tip of his polished boot.

“Why are you surprised at me?” Ivan asked abruptly and sullenly, doing his utmost to restrain himself. He suddenly realized with disgust that he was feeling intense curiosity and would not, on any account, have gone away without satisfying it.

“Why don’t you go to Tchermashnya, sir?” Smerdyakov suddenly raised his eyes and smiled familiarly. “Why I smile you must understand for yourself, if you are a clever man,” his screwed-up left eye seemed to say.
“Why should I go to Tchermashnya?” Ivan asked in surprise.
Smerdyakov was silent again.

“Fyodor Pavlovitch himself has begged you so much to,” he said at last, slowly, and apparently attaching no importance to his answer. “I put you off with a secondary reason,” he seemed to suggest, “simply to say something.”
“Damn you! Say what you want!” Ivan cried angrily at last, going from meekness to violence.
Smerdyakov drew his right foot up to his left, pulled himself upright, but still looked at him with the same calm and the same little smile.
“Substantially nothing—but just by way of conversation.”

Another silence followed. They did not speak for nearly a minute. Ivan knew that he ought to get up and show anger, and Smerdyakov stood before him, seeming to wait and see whether he would be angry or not. So at least it seemed to Ivan. At last he moved to get up. Smerdyakov seemed to seize the moment.
“I’m in an awful position, Ivan Fyodorovitch. I don’t know how to help myself,” he said resolutely and distinctly, and at his last word he sighed. Ivan Fyodorovitch sat down again.

“They are both utterly crazy, they are no better than little children,” Smerdyakov went on. “I am speaking of your parent and your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Any minute now Fyodor Pavlovitch will get up and start worrying me, ‘Has she come? Why hasn’t she come?’ and so on every minute till midnight and even after midnight. And if Agrafena Alexandrovna doesn’t come (for very likely she does not mean to come at all) then he will be at me again tomorrow morning, ‘Why hasn’t she come? When will she come?’—as though I were to blame for it. On the other side it’s no better. As soon as it gets dark, or even before, your brother will appear with his gun in his hands: ‘Look out, you rogue, you soup-maker. If you miss her and don’t let me know she’s been—I’ll kill you before anyone else.’ When the night is over, in the morning, he, too, like Fyodor Pavlovitch, begins worrying me to death. ‘Why hasn’t she come? Will she come soon?’ And he, too, thinks me to blame because his lady hasn’t come. And every day and every hour they get angrier and angrier, so that I sometimes think I shall kill myself in fright. I can’t depend on them, sir.”
“And why have you meddled? Why did you start spying for Dmitri Fyodorovitch?” said Ivan irritably.

“How could I help meddling? Though, indeed, I haven’t meddled at all, if you want to know the truth of the matter. I kept quiet from the very beginning, not daring to answer, but he picked me out to be his servant. He has had only one thing to say since: ‘I’ll kill you, you scoundrel, if you miss her.’ I feel certain, sir, that I shall have a long fit tomorrow.”
“What do you mean by ‘a long fit’?”

“A long fit, lasting a long time—several hours, or perhaps a day or two. Once it went on for three days. I fell from the garret that time. The convulsions stopped and then began again, and for three days I couldn’t come back to my senses. Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Herzenstube, the doctor here, and he put ice on my head and tried another remedy too.... I might have died.”
“But they say one can’t tell with epilepsy when a fit is coming. What makes you say you will have one tomorrow?” Ivan inquired, with a peculiar, irritable curiosity.
“That’s just so. You can’t tell beforehand.”
“Besides, you fell from the garret then.”
“I climb up to the garret every day. I might fall from the garret again tomorrow. And if not, I might fall down the cellar steps. I have to go into the cellar every day, too.”
Ivan took a long look at him.
“You are talking nonsense, I see, and I don’t quite understand you,” he said softly, but with a sort of menace. “Do you mean to pretend to be ill tomorrow for three days, eh?”
Smerdyakov had been looking at the ground again and playing with the toe of his right foot. Now he set the foot down, moved the left one forward, and, grinning, said:

“If I were able to play such a trick, that is, pretend to have a fit—and it would not be difficult for a man used to them—I should have a perfect right to use such a means to save myself from death. For even if Agrafena Alexandrovna comes to see his father while I am ill, his honor can’t blame a sick man for not telling him. He’d be ashamed to.”
